conflicts.note: Best resolved by separating 'introduction of the model' (1965 production / 1963 prototypes) from 'best-known generation' (1968-style dial). The Blomman piece explicitly flags JLC's own brand narrative as imprecise.
positions: Several sources say production began in 1965 after 1963 prototypes (Mstanga, Blomman, Hairspring, Fratello, S.Song).
Hour Markers and a few brand summaries cite 1968 / 1962 as the 'introduction' year — JLC's own marketing has historically framed 1968 as the launch.

conflicts.note: Both accounts agree the name was a US-market choice and was not used in period European catalogues (the 1965 doc calls it a 'Deep Sea Skin Diver').
positions: Mstanga: the US division wanted a name evoking the spirit of adventure (water, polar, space).
Fratello and Watchonista: the name was chosen for the US market and was likely inspired by the Cold War-era Polaris submarine-launched ballistic missile.

conflicts.note: The detailed archival numbers come from a single collector source; treat the year-by-year split as best-available rather than canonical.
positions: Mstanga's archival breakdown: 1,150 pieces in 1968 (plus the 9 from 1967 and 55 Calypso in 1970), summing to 1,214 'second-generation' style.
Some general references describe the 1968 batch as 'the lion's share' without itemising.

conflicts.note: Minor discrepancy in end-of-production date; both agree it was a brief, design-radically-different successor on calibre 916.
positions: Fratello / Swisswatches: Memovox Polaris II / E870 produced 1970–1971, with the broader Plongeur platform continuing slightly later.

consensus.claim: The Memovox Polaris reference E859 entered serial production in 1965 after roughly 50 prototypes were built in 1963, and remained in production until around 1970.
Total E859 production was 1,714 watches (not counting the ~50 prototypes), making it a genuinely rare model despite its outsized cultural footprint.
Mstanga's archival breakdown gives 500 units in 1965, 9 in 1967, 1,150 in 1968 and 55 of the controversial Calypso-hand variant in 1970, with the 1968 batch the dominant production year.
The case is a 42mm Piquerez (EPSA) compressor design whose seals tighten under pressure, with water resistance rated to 200 metres.

The case is fitted with a three-layer ('triple') caseback: an inner sealing layer, a brass resonator and an outer shield perforated with 16 holes, designed so the alarm can be heard and felt underwater.
The E859 has three quadrille-decorated crowns: top for winding/setting the alarm (and quick-set date), middle for the internal rotating dive bezel, lower for winding the movement and setting time.
The E859 is powered by the automatic bumper-rotor calibre K825, a 17-jewel movement shared with other Memovox alarm models of the era.
Dials were signed either 'Jaeger-LeCoultre' (Europe) or 'LeCoultre' (US market); the LeCoultre signature was never the basis for the 2008 Tribute to Polaris re-edition.
The original Polaris had no external bezel; the elapsed-time scale rotates internally under the deeply domed Hesalite crystal, giving the dial its characteristic 'aquarium' appearance.

The 1965 first-generation dial uses thin applied indices with small lume plots and gilt printing, while the later (1968-style) dial introduces large trapezoidal tritium markers for stronger underwater legibility.

The E859 was conceived as a true tool dive watch: the alarm was meant as a dive-time / decompression reminder, audible and tactile underwater — a different solution to the same problem solved by external rotating bezels on competitors.
The Polaris was lineage-descended from the Memovox Deep Sea (ref. E857) of 1959, the first automatic dive alarm wristwatch, of which roughly 1,000+ pieces were made.

The 'Polaris' name was a US-market designation; period LeCoultre catalogues from 1965 referred to the watch as a 'Deep Sea Skin Diver,' and the name was reportedly chosen to evoke an adventurous, Cold-War-era spirit (and is widely tied to the Polaris submarine-launched missile).
The original Polaris was usually delivered on a Tropic-style rubber strap; a steel bracelet by J.B. Champion (USA) was offered, primarily for the US market, and is now hard to find.
Service crowns can be distinguished from originals by a circle around the quadrille decoration; original crowns have the cross-hatched pattern without that surrounding ring.

For collectability, the dial signature should be matched by the movement bridge signature (LeCoultre with LeCoultre, Jaeger-LeCoultre with Jaeger-LeCoultre); the inner caseback is always marked 'LeCoultre' regardless of the dial.
The Memovox Polaris II (ref. E870 / 14.2320) succeeded the original in 1970–71 with an oval case, external bezel and the new high-beat calibre 916; it ran alongside, then replaced, the E859.
JLC revived the Polaris name in 2008 with the Memovox Tribute to Polaris, a faithful 42mm re-edition limited to 768 pieces, which served as the bridge between the vintage and modern eras.

At SIHH 2018 JLC relaunched Polaris as a full collection: Automatic (41mm, cal. 898/1), Date (42mm, cal. 899/1, 200m), Memovox (42mm, cal. 956, 200m, 1,000-piece LE), Chronograph (42mm, cal. 751) and Chronograph World Time (44mm titanium, cal. 752).

The modern Polaris Memovox (Q9038670) retains the alarm function via calibre 956, with 200m water resistance and triple-crown layout, and was issued as a 1,000-piece limited edition to mark the 50th anniversary.

The 2020 Polaris Mariner Memovox pushed the line back into proper professional dive territory with 300m water resistance, a screw-down crown, a blue sunray-and-grained dial with orange accents, and a sapphire caseback exposing the calibre 956's alarm hammer.

The modern Polaris Date (Q9068670 series) follows the vintage cues most closely: trapezoidal indices, four Arabic numerals, vanilla-toned lume, internal bezel, dual compressor-style crowns, and an engraved scuba diver on the caseback echoing the period inner caseback marking.
The modern Polaris dial architecture combines three textures — sunray-brushed centre, grained hour chapter, opaline inner bezel — a deliberate signature across the 2018+ collection.

marks.explanation: Inner sealing layer, brass resonator and an outer shield drilled with 16 holes — purpose-built to let the alarm sound out underwater. The caseback bears the Compressor diving-helmet logo.

marks.explanation: Top = alarm wind/set (and quick-set date), middle = internal rotating bezel, bottom = movement winding and time-setting. Originals have a clean cross-hatched 'quadrille' field; service replacements are recognisable by an extra ring around the pattern.
marks.name: Three quadrille-decorated crowns

marks.explanation: The elapsed-time/dive scale rotates inside the case under a deeply domed Hesalite crystal, giving the dial its often-cited 'aquarium' look — set via the middle crown.
marks.name: No external bezel — internal rotating dive scale

marks.explanation: 42mm super-compressor case where the caseback sealing rings tighten as ambient pressure rises — more secure with depth.
marks.name: Piquerez (EPSA) compressor case

marks.explanation: European/Swiss-market dials are signed 'Jaeger-LeCoultre'; US-market dials are signed 'LeCoultre' only. The inner caseback is marked 'LeCoultre' regardless, and the movement bridge should ideally match the dial signature.
marks.name: Dial signature: 'Jaeger-LeCoultre' vs 'LeCoultre'

marks.explanation: The inner caseback carries a month-year stamp (e.g. '5-65' for May 1965, '5-68' for May 1968) — a key authenticity marker, with the 1967 batch of just 9 pieces stamped accordingly.

marks.explanation: First-generation (1965) dials use thin applied indices, small lume plots, and either dauphine or sword hands. The 1968-style dial introduces large trapezoidal tritium markers and consistent baton hands for stronger underwater legibility.
marks.name: Dial-generation hand and index shift

marks.explanation: 17-jewel automatic bumper-rotor alarm movement; the Polaris uses the same calibre family as other Memovox alarms of the era — the 'bumper' rotor was retained because a free rotor would interfere with the alarm hammer striking the caseback.

model_context: The Jaeger-LeCoultre Polaris sits within JLC's sports-watch lineage, anchored by the reference E859 — a Memovox-based dive watch developed from 1963, with serial production from 1965 to roughly 1970. It grew out of the Memovox Deep Sea (ref. E857) of 1959, the first automatic dive alarm wristwatch, and used JLC's expertise in the alarm complication to solve a diver's core problem: how do you know when to surface? The Polaris answered with an audible alarm that could be heard and felt underwater, housed in a 42mm Piquerez (EPSA) compressor case with a three-layer caseback featuring 16 holes drilled in the outermost layer to let the sound escape. Three crowns — alarm, internal bezel, time/date — and a bezel-less, deeply domed Hesalite crystal gave the dial an unusual 'aquarium' look that has defined the watch's identity ever since. Total E859 production was modest at 1,714 pieces (plus around 50 prototypes), split across dial generations and the two market signatures: 'Jaeger-LeCoultre' (Europe/Switzerland) and 'LeCoultre' (US, where the Polaris name actually originated, reportedly evoking the Cold-War spirit of adventure and the Polaris missile). After the original Polaris faded in the early 1970s — succeeded briefly by the radically different Polaris II / E870 — the name slept for decades, surfacing only in tribute editions (notably the 2008 Memovox Tribute to Polaris, 768 pieces, and a 2013 platinum tribute) before JLC relaunched Polaris as a full sports-watch collection at SIHH 2018. Today the Polaris is positioned as JLC's sportier, more accessible everyday line alongside the Reverso and Master Control, with Date, Automatic, Chronograph, World Time, Memovox, and more recently Mariner, Geographic and Perpetual Calendar variants.

module_candidates.rationale: The 1959 ancestor of the Polaris — the first automatic dive alarm wristwatch and the direct lineage step into the E859. Deserves its own page covering Mr Lowe's proposal, the US-market 'playful script' dial, the I.C. Rapoport ownership story, and the way it defined JLC's alternative answer to the dive watch (alarm instead of bezel).

The radically different 1970–71 successor: oval Nardin/Narval case, calibre 916 high-beat with free rotor, external bezel, single-layer resonator caseback. Distinct enough mechanically and stylistically to warrant its own reference page.

The 768-piece bridge between vintage and modern — the watch that re-established the Polaris name a full decade before the 2018 relaunch. Documented market behaviour, Goodwood-replica framing, and concrete reference number make it a clean standalone page.

module_candidates.rationale: The two modern alarm divers — the 2018 1,000-piece LE and the 2020 Mariner with 300m WR and sapphire caseback — share the calibre 956 but differ enough in spec and intent to anchor their own page on how the alarm complication was re-engineered for the modern era.

The Polaris is the sports child of a much larger family that includes the Memovox Wrist Alarm (1950), the E853/E855 calendar Memovox, the Snowdrop, the TV-Screen, the Master Compressor Memovox (2002) and today's Master Control Memovox. A family-level page gives the Polaris its proper context.

The compressor patent shaped a generation of dive watches across many brands; a module on EPSA Piquerez compressor cases — what they are, how the seal-under-pressure system works, who else used them — would support both the E859 page and adjacent dive-watch pages.

stories.title: Bertram S. Lowe and the New York proposal
stories.why: The Polaris exists because the US head of LeCoultre Watch Inc., Bertram S. Lowe, wrote to the JLC board in 1959/1961 proposing a diver's watch with an alarm — and later proposed using a compressor case. The watch's identity was literally shaped by its American market.

stories.title: The 1965 catalogue calls it a 'Deep Sea Skin Diver'
stories.why: Period catalogue evidence shows the 'Polaris' name was a later, US-driven label. The watch was originally pitched in print as 'the only one of its kind in the world' — the only dive watch with both alarm AND automatic winding, contrasted with the Vulcain diver's manual alarm.

stories.title: The 9 pieces of 1967
stories.why: Out of 1,714 total E859s, just 9 were assembled in 1967 — reportedly as test pieces for the bolder, more legible dial that would become the dominant 1968 look. Cases from that year carry '67' stamped on the inner caseback.

stories.title: The Calypso-hands variant of 1970
stories.why: A controversial 55-piece run with unusual 'Calypso' hands was produced in 1970 — collectors generally treat it as the awkward outlier of the line.

stories.title: Why a bumper rotor — and not a full rotor
stories.why: The Memovox alarm works by a hammer striking a post connected to the caseback; a full 360° rotor would foul that mechanism. JLC stuck with a bumper-style oscillating weight (limited swing, coiled springs to bounce off) — also useful as a way to enter automatic territory without infringing Rolex's full-rotor patent.

stories.title: Benedict Cumberbatch and 'In a Breath'
stories.why: Cumberbatch, a JLC brand ambassador, wore the modern Polaris Mariner Memovox while making the short film 'In a Breath', and has called it one of his favourite timepieces.

stories.title: The Lucky 13 Polaris Date
stories.why: A unique Polaris Date created in 2019 to celebrate the 13 complications of JLC's Hybris Mechanica à Grande Sonnerie, with a '13' engraved on the rotor — a one-off auctioned that December.

stories.title: The Memovox Polaris II — the strange one
stories.why: Often forgotten, the 1970–71 Polaris II / E870 swapped the iconic look for an oval case, vivid blue 70s-style dial, external bezel and the new high-beat calibre 916 — radically different in spirit from the E859 it ran alongside.
